Terrain and site conditions \u2014 approach"},{"line":11,"text":""},{"line":12,"text":"**Ground form.** The plot is flat and level, which is the single most useful fact"},{"line":13,"text":"here: no significant cut-and-fill, no retaining structures, no stepped"},{"line":14,"text":"foundations, and no slope-stability question. The design consequence is that the"},{"line":15,"text":"whole feasibility risk shifts from *earthworks* to *water*. A level site with"},{"line":16,"text":"layered soil drains poorly by nature, so the survey approach is:"},{"line":17,"text":""},{"line":18,"text":"1. **Confirm the stratigraphy before anything else.** \"Stratified soil, generally"},{"line":19,"text":"   suitable for shallow spread footings\" is a green light for the foundation"},{"line":20,"text":"   *type*, not a substitute for the bearing check. I would require a borehole /"},{"line":21,"text":"   trial-pit campaign (minimum 3\u20134 pits across the 60 m grid, plus one at the"},{"line":22,"text":"   cafeteria corner) to establish: depth and thickness of each layer, the"},{"line":23,"text":"   bearing stratum actually selected, its allowable bearing pressure, and"},{"line":24,"text":"   whether any layer is shrinkable clay, loose fill, or organic."},{"line":25,"text":"2. **Check for a perched water table.** Layered soils commonly hold water on top"},{"line":26,"text":"   of a less permeable stratum. This matters more than the regional water table:"},{"line":27,"text":"   it drives foundation depth, drainage design, and whether a basement or"},{"line":28,"text":"   semi-basement is even worth considering (my answer: no \u2014 see \u00a73)."},{"line":29,"text":"3. **Differential settlement across layer boundaries.** Where the bearing"},{"line":30,"text":"   stratum changes depth across the footprint, footings on either side can settle"},{"line":31,"text":"   differently. Mitigation is cheap at this stage: keep the building on one"},{"line":32,"text":"   consistent founding level where possible, use a reinforced ground beam /"},{"line":33,"text":"   tie-beam grid to stitch pad footings together, and keep the cafeteria (the"},{"line":34,"text":"   heaviest, most service-dense block) on the most uniform part of the plot."},{"line":35,"text":"4. **Positive drainage as a design requirement, not an afterthought.** Flat"},{"line":36,"text":"   ground means the building must be raised on a plinth (I would use ~450\u2013600 mm"},{"line":37,"text":"   above surrounding finished level) with a perimeter apron and falls away from"},{"line":38,"text":"   the building. Surface water strategy: perimeter trench drains / slot drains,"},{"line":39,"text":"   falls on all hardstanding, and either connection to the campus storm network"},{"line":40,"text":"   or \u2014 if the soil permeability allows \u2014 soakaways. If the upper layer is"},{"line":41,"text":"   clayey, soakaways are out and attenuation/connection is in; that decision"},{"line":42,"text":"   follows directly from the borehole log."},{"line":43,"text":"5. **Service and access check.** Confirm the incoming water main size and"},{"line":44,"text":"   pressure (a cafeteria kitchen is a heavy intermittent water user), the"},{"line":45,"text":"   electrical supply capacity, and the foul drainage invert depth at the plot"},{"line":46,"text":"   boundary. A cafeteria grease-laden waste stream needs a grease trap and a"},{"line":47,"text":"   dedicated foul run \u2014 this is a site-level constraint, not a fit-out detail."},{"line":48,"text":""},{"line":49,"text":"**Foundations (decision).** Standard shallow **reinforced-concrete pad footings"},{"line":50,"text":"under columns and strip footings under load-bearing walls**, founded on the"},{"line":51,"text":"verified bearing stratum, with a reinforced ground-beam grid tying the pads"},{"line":52,"text":"together. No piling is anticipated on the given information; I would hold piling"},{"line":53,"text":"in reserve only if the boreholes reveal a soft layer thicker than ~2 m beneath"},{"line":54,"text":"the cafeteria or a high perched water table."},{"line":55,"text":""},{"line":56,"text":"---"},{"line":57,"text":""},{"line":58,"text":"## 2. Zoning and footprint concept"},{"line":59,"text":""},{"line":60,"text":"Total plot \u22483,600 m\u00b2. I would not build out the whole plot \u2014 a mid-sized faculty"},{"line":61,"text":"needs external circulation, daylight, and a service yard."},{"line":62,"text":""},{"line":63,"text":"**Indicative massing:** a two- to three-storey main academic block with a"},{"line":64,"text":"footprint of roughly **1,600\u20131,900 m\u00b2**, leaving ~45\u201355 % of the plot as"},{"line":65,"text":"hardstanding, planting, and circulation."},{"line":66,"text":""},{"line":67,"text":"Zoning, in plan:"},{"line":68,"text":""},{"line":69,"text":"- **Academic block (north / quiet side):** lecture halls and classrooms stacked"},{"line":70,"text":"  over two or three floors. Large rooms want long spans and few columns, so this"},{"line":71,"text":"  block drives the structural grid. Ground floor gets the largest halls (easiest"},{"line":72,"text":"  for egress and for moving equipment); upper floors get smaller classrooms and"},{"line":73,"text":"  seminar rooms."},{"line":74,"text":"- **Staff offices (adjacent to academic block, quieter edge):** cellular offices"},{"line":75,"text":"  and small meeting rooms, naturally ventilated where possible, on a shallower"},{"line":76,"text":"  span grid. Grouped so they can be compartmented and locked down separately"},{"line":77,"text":"  from teaching space."},{"line":78,"text":"- **Cafeteria / canteen (separate wing, ground floor, own entrance):** placed at"},{"line":79,"text":"  the plot edge nearest the main pedestrian flow, with a **dedicated service"},{"line":80,"text":"  yard, delivery access, and bin/grease-trap zone** on the opposite face. It is"},{"line":81,"text":"  deliberately a *separate wing* rather than a room inside the academic block:"},{"line":82,"text":"  this isolates kitchen fire risk, grease and odour, and heavy water use from the"},{"line":83,"text":"  teaching environment, and lets the dining hall be a tall, column-free,"},{"line":84,"text":"  daylit volume."},{"line":85,"text":"- **Circulation spine:** a single covered spine linking the three zones, doubling"},{"line":86,"text":"  as the primary escape route and as the accessible route (level thresholds"},{"line":87,"text":"  throughout, lift + stair core at the junction of academic and office blocks)."},{"line":88,"text":"- **External:** short-stay drop-off and accessible parking at the entrance edge,"},{"line":89,"text":"  cycle parking, and a service route that does not cross the student entrance."},{"line":90,"text":""},{"line":91,"text":"**Why this zoning:** it separates the three functional risk profiles \u2014 quiet"},{"line":92,"text":"teaching, cellular office work, and a wet, hot, greasy, high-occupancy food"},{"line":93,"text":"operation \u2014 so that each can be built with the materials and fire strategy it"},{"line":94,"text":"actually needs, instead of compromising one for the others."},{"line":95,"text":""},{"line":96,"text":"---"},{"line":97,"text":""},{"line":98,"text":"## 3. Primary construction materials"},{"line":99,"text":""},{"line":100,"text":"**General building \u2014 decision: reinforced-concrete frame with masonry infill.**"},{"line":101,"text":""},{"line":102,"text":"- **Structure:** in-situ reinforced-concrete columns

Reading the site"},{"line":10,"text":""},{"line":11,"text":"The plot is not a flat platform with a building on it; the 18 m cross-fall is the dominant design fact. At 100 m up-slope with 18 m of rise, the average grade is ~18%, which is beyond comfortable pedestrian route gradients (typically 1:20 / 5% preferred, 1:12 / 8.3% absolute maximum for ramps) and well beyond accessible route limits over any distance. That single number drives the whole concept: **the building must absorb the level change internally rather than the site being flattened to suit it.**"},{"line":12,"text":""},{"line":13,"text":"Key consequences:"},{"line":14,"text":""},{"line":15,"text":"- **Cut-and-fill balance is the first economic question.** A single-level platform would require either ~18 m of cut at the uphill edge or ~18 m of fill at the downhill edge \u2014 both are large earthworks, and deep fill on a slope is a settlement and stability liability. I will not pursue a single platform."},{"line":16,"text":"- **Terracing is the organising move.** Two or three terraces, each tied to a building level, keeps cut and fill local and modest, and lets each terrace drain to its own edge."},{"line":17,"text":"- **Retaining is unavoidable** at every terrace edge and along the uphill cut face. These are structural elements, not landscape trim, and they need geotechnical design (see \u00a72)."},{"line":18,"text":"- **Drainage is a slope problem, not a roof problem.** Surface water arriving from up-slope must be intercepted *above* the building and carried around it in a cut-off drain; water falling on terraces must be collected and discharged to a controlled outfall, not allowed to sheet down the slope face. Uncontrolled down-slope discharge is the classic trigger for slope instability and for undermining retaining wall foundations."},{"line":19,"text":"- **Access gradient.** Vehicle access (service, deliveries, ambulance/fire) needs a route at or below ~1:8 (12.5%) with a short 1:6 (16.7%) maximum only if unavoidable, and it must be a *route*, not a ramp \u2014 so the access road should run diagonally across the slope (traversing) rather than straight up it. Pedestrian accessible routes should be near-level within each terrace, with the level change taken by lifts and by short, generously-landing ramps or stepped routes with a parallel accessible alternative."},{"line":20,"text":""},{"line":21,"text":"## 2. Geotechnical approach"},{"line":22,"text":""},{"line":23,"text":"Given the slope, the geotechnical scope is materially larger than a flat-site survey:"},{"line":24,"text":""},{"line":25,"text":"1. **Ground investigation before any layout is fixed.** Boreholes/test pits on a grid across the whole footprint *and* across the terrace edges and retaining lines \u2014 not one central hole. I need the depth to a competent bearing stratum, the presence and dip of any weaker layer, groundwater level and its seasonal variation, and the shear strength parameters for slope stability analysis."},{"line":26,"text":"2. **Slope stability analysis** for both the existing slope and the post-construction slope, including the temporary condition during excavation (a cut face is at its most vulnerable before the building and drainage are in). Global stability, not just local bearing, governs here."},{"line":27,"text":"3. **Retaining walls** designed for at-rest or higher earth pressures (a restrained wall against a slope cannot be assumed to develop active pressure), with proper drainage behind the wall (filter drain + weep outlets), and founded below the zone of seasonal moisture movement. Where walls are tall or the retained slope is significant, consider soil-nailed or anchored solutions rather than a simple cantilever."},{"line":28,"text":"4. **Foundations.** I expect to step footings down the slope, keeping column bases on consistent strata and founding below the frost/seasonal-movement zone. This is exactly the caution raised by the Faculty of Arts (see \u00a76) and it applies with force on a sloping, layered profile."},{"line":29,"text":"5. **Movement tolerance.** Ground-floor slabs, drainage runs and services connections should be detailed to tolerate small differential movement \u2014 movement joints, flexible couplings, and falls that still work if a slab settles a few millimetres."},{"line":30,"text":""},{"line":31,"text":"## 3. Zoning and footprint concept"},{"line":32,"text":""},{"line":33,"text":"**Concept: a stepped spine with terraced wings.**"},{"line":34,"text":""},{"line":35,"text":"- **Spine block** running *across* the slope (along the contour) at mid-height \u2014 this is the most efficient orientation because a building running along the contour needs the least cut/fill for a given length, and it gives the longest dimension of the building the gentlest ground relationship."},{"line":36,"text":"- **Two terraces** either side of the spine, at different levels, connected internally by the spine's stairs and lifts. ## 1. Site, foundations and drainage — final

The site is flat and level with stratified soil. Nothing in any peer survey
changes this reading: four of the six faculties (Medicine, Computing, Business,
Law, Arts) were given the same flat, layered site, and the one peer on a
different site (Engineering, a hillside plot) confirms rather than contradicts
the flat-site logic — its slope-specific measures (terracing, retaining walls,
slope-stability analysis, cut-off drains) are simply not applicable here.

**Foundations (final decision).** Shallow **reinforced-concrete pad footings**
under columns and **strip footings** under load-bearing walls, founded on the
verified bearing stratum, tied together by a **reinforced ground-beam /
tie-beam grid**. No piling is anticipated; piling is held in reserve only if the
ground investigation reveals a soft layer thicker than ~2 m beneath the
cafeteria or a high perched water table.

**Ground investigation (final scope).** A borehole / trial-pit grid across the
**whole footprint** — not one central hole — with a minimum of 3–4 pits on the
60 m grid **plus a dedicated pit at the cafeteria corner**. The investigation
must establish, before foundation design is fixed: the depth and thickness of
each stratum; the bearing stratum actually selected and its allowable bearing
pressure; whether any layer is shrinkable clay, loose fill or organic; the
presence of a perched water table; and (added after reading the Arts survey)
**groundwater level and seasonal variation, sulphate/aggressive ground
chemistry (which sets the concrete mix and buried-service specification), and
any made ground or buried obstructions from previous use.**

**Differential settlement (final position).** The ground-beam/tie-beam grid is a
firm part of the foundation decision, not an option. Column bases are kept on a
single stratum where possible and stepped or deepened across a transition. The
cafeteria — the heaviest, most service-dense block — is kept on the most uniform
part of the plot. Ground-floor slabs and drainage are detailed to tolerate small
differential movement: movement joints, flexible service connections, and slab
reinforcement detailed for it.

**Drainage and levels (final).** The building sits on a **plinth ~450–600 mm
above surrounding finished level**, with a perimeter apron and falls away from
the building on all sides. Surface water is collected by perimeter trench/slot
drains and a positive piped storm system to the site outfall; because the site
is flat, the **outfall invert and capacity govern the design** and must be
confirmed before the footprint is frozen. Attenuation (below-ground crate
storage or a shallow basin) is assumed to be required. Soakaways are used only
if the borehole log shows the upper layer is permeable; if it is clayey,
attenuation/connection is the answer. **All external circulation is step-free
(max 1:20 ramps where levels change).**

**No basement.** Ruled out at feasibility: on a flat, layered site with a
possible perched water table it buys little and adds waterproofing, dewatering
and settlement risk.

**Massing.** A two- to three-storey main academic block with a footprint of
roughly **1,600–1,900 m²**, leaving ~45–55 % of the plot as hardstanding,

ground level**.

differential movement: movement joints, flexible service connections, and slab
reinforcement detailed for it.

**Drainage and levels (final).** The building sits on a **plinth ~450–600 mm
above surrounding finished level**, with a perimeter apron and falls away from
the building on all sides. Surface water is collected by perimeter trench/slot
drains and a positive piped storm system to the site outfall; because the site
is flat, the **outfall invert and capacity govern the design** and must be
confirmed before the footprint is frozen. Attenuation (below-ground crate
storage or a shallow basin) is assumed to be required. Soakaways are used only
if the borehole log shows the upper layer is permeable; if it is clayey,
attenuation/connection is the answer. **All external circulation is step-free
(max 1:20 ramps where levels change).**

**No basement.** Ruled out at feasibility: on a flat, layered site with a
possible perched water table it buys little and adds waterproofing, dewatering
and settlement risk.

---

## 2. Footprint and zoning — final

**Massing.** A two- to three-storey main academic block with a footprint of
roughly **1,600–1,900 m²**, leaving ~45–55 % of the plot as hardstanding,
planting and circulation. The cafeteria is a **separate single-storey wing at
ground level**.

**Zoning, in plan:**

- **Academic block (north / quiet side).** Lecture halls and classrooms stacked
  over two or three floors. Ground floor takes the largest halls (easiest for
  egress and for moving equipment); upper floors take smaller classrooms and
  seminar rooms. This block drives the structural grid because large rooms want
  long spans and few columns.
- **Staff offices (adjacent to the academic block, quieter edge).** Cellular
  offices and small meeting rooms on a shallower span grid, grouped so they can
  be compartmented and locked down separately from teaching space.
- **Cafeteria / canteen (separate wing, ground floor, own external entrance).**
  Placed at the plot edge nearest the main pedestrian flow, with a **dedicated
  service yard, delivery access and bin/grease-trap zone on the opposite face**.
  It is deliberately a separate wing rather than a room inside the academic
  block: this isolates kitchen fire risk, grease and odour, and heavy water use
  from the teaching environment, and lets the dining hall be a tall,
  column-free, daylit volume.
- **Circulation spine.** A single covered spine links the three zones, doubling
  as the primary escape route and the accessible route (level thresholds
  throughout; lift + stair core at the junction of the academic and office
  blocks).
- **External.** Short-stay drop-off and accessible parking at the entrance edge,
  cycle parking, and a service route that does not cross the student entrance.

**Zoning refinements adopted from peer surveys (see §5):**

- The cafeteria is planned as a **campus-facing pavilion**: it has its own
  external door, is reachable without entering the teaching block, and is
  designed to **operate outside faculty hours** (Law survey). It is also
  **structurally and services-independent**, so it can be built as a second
  phase without disrupting teaching (Law survey).
- The **kitchen grease-duct route is reserved in the zoning layout from the
  outset**: a short, direct route to a roof termination, with a dedicated
  vertical shaft, because the duct and its fire-rated enclosure drive
  ceiling-void depth, roof penetrations and shaft locations (Computing, Law,
  Business, Engineering surveys — all four converge on this).
- The **dining hall is separated from the stiff kitchen box by a movement/fire
  joint**, so the long-span dining volume and the cellular kitchen do not fight
  each other (Law survey).
- **Escape routes from the dining hall lead directly to outside, not through
  the kitchen** (Law survey).
- The cafeteria glazing is oriented to take daylight **without direct afternoon
  sun on the dining area**, with deep overhangs or external shading on the
  sun-facing elevations (Computing survey).

---

## 3. Primary construction materials — general building (final)

**Structure: in-situ reinforced-concrete frame with masonry infill.** RC
columns, beams and slabs. Reasons: it suits the layered-soil shallow-footing
solution directly (the continuous RC frame ties into the ground-beam grid and
tolerates minor differential movement); it is inherently fire-resistant with no
applied protection; it gives good acoustic separation between stacked lecture
halls; and it is robust and low-maintenance in a high-traffic institutional
building. Long-span lecture halls are handled with deeper RC beams or a
ribbed/voided slab rather than by changing material.

**External walls:** clay or concrete masonry infill with a drained and
ventilated rainscreen or a rendered insulated cavity. Cavity insulation plus
masonry gives thermal mass, which reduces peak cooling load.

**Roof:** insulated RC slab with a waterproof membrane and protected finish, or
a ventilated pitched roof over the academic block. Flat, well-drained and
walkable for maintenance access.
